[MUQATIL:11:86-88/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The people mock Shuayb, asking if his prayers command them to abandon the idols their fathers worshipped.
[MUQATIL:11:86-88/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | They claim they may do as they wish with their money, either reducing measures and weights or giving full measure.
[MUQATIL:11:86-88/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | In mockery, they call Shuayb a fool by saying patient and rightly guided, meaning foolish and astray.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sibawayh raises the verb after حتى when it is detached from an asserted first action already completed; he uses the subjunctive when entry is intended as the endpoint.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With كان, an adverb like أمس can complete the first clause and permit raising after حتى; without a predicate for كان, that analysis fails.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | He rejects the claim that the subjunctive follows merely because the speaker is uncertain; even an explicit uncertainty adjunct does not require it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | He criticizes grammarians who force the subjunctive to avoid a perceived inversion: Arabs still raise after قد سرت.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With negated or rare little travel, raising presents entry as separate, while the subjunctive makes it the endpoint; قلما can negate many trips or much travel in one trip.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil says إنما سرت حتى أدخلها is awkward unless the trip is belittled; the wording otherwise gives no sign that the travel ended before entry.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The verb after حتى does not share the syntactic slot of the first verb as a verb after فاء does; it is detached like a clause after إذا or an introductory particle.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After a nonasserted clause, حتى takes only the subjunctive because it reverts to أن or كي instead of acting as a clause-initial connector.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أيهم سار حتى يدخلها allows raising because travel and entry are already asserted and only the actor is queried; أسرت حتى تدخلها requires subjunctive because no trip was affirmed.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالرفعفيمااتصلبالأولكاتصالهms372بالفاءوماانتصبلأنهغاية#472/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In some contexts the present نفعل can stand for past فعلنا; a Sululi poem illustrates this, and أسير likewise means سرت when intended as past.
[FARRA:v2p26/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The people address Shuʿayb with الحليم الرشيد sarcastically.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p311#2/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · الأعمش | reports | Al-Aʿmash explains “your prayers” as “your recitation.”
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p118/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Shuʿayb's people call him forbearing and prudent sarcastically, as one might call an idiot intelligent or a fool forbearing.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p118/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The poet's address 'O forbearing one' is sarcastic, accusing the person of failing to act gently.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p255/r6] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The people of Shuʿayb use الصلاة to mean religion when they mockingly ask whether it commands him to abandon ancestral worship.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p255/r7] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | reports | الصلاة is also said to mean recitation in the question about Shuʿayb.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p41/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | An anonymous poem jussives وأستدرج by carrying over the syntactic position of أصالحكم, understood without the preceding لعلي.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p41/r10] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The codex writes ما نشؤا with wāw after alif in Shuʿayb's verse, while the same form elsewhere lacks wāw, without a difference in meaning.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p41/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Ibn Qutayba says disputed forms either follow accepted grammar or reflect scribal spelling; in the first case Quran has no grammatical error, and in the second the scribe's fault is not the Messenger's.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p41/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · عائشة | reports | Aisha is cited for the view that some disputed forms are mistakes made by the copyist.
[TAB-FULL:v12p545/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The people ask whether Shuaib's prayer commands them to abandon the idols and images worshipped by their fathers.
[TAB-FULL:v12p545/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | They object to being stopped from doing as they wished with their money, including clipping coins and shorting people in measure and weight.
[TAB-FULL:v12p545/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | A forbearing person is not driven by anger to do what he would not do while calm.
[TAB-FULL:v12p545/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | They call him soundly guided because he directs them to abandon idol worship.
[TAB-FULL:v12p545/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · زيد بن أسلم | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam reports that Shuaib prohibited clipping or cutting dirhams; the transmitter is unsure which wording he used.
[TAB-FULL:v12p545/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · محمد بن كعب القرظي | reports | Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi says Shuaib's people were punished for cutting dirhams, citing their objection in this verse.
[TAB-FULL:v12p545/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says Shuaib prohibited cutting dinars and dirhams, while the people claimed they could cut, burn, or discard their own money as they wished.
[TAB-FULL:v12p546#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الأعمش | reports | Al-Aʿmash glosses Shuaib's prayer as his recitation.
[TAB-FULL:v12p546#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض البصريين | reports | The Basran reading supplies a second أن نترك: does your prayer command us to abandon our fathers' worship or to abandon doing as we please with our wealth?
[TAB-FULL:v12p546#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض الكوفيين | reports | Some Kufans agree with that parse and offer another: the question contrasts prayer commanding one thing with forbidding another, and attaches the second phrase to ما يعبد.
[TAB-FULL:v12p546#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض الكوفيين | reports | In the alternative Kufan parse, the first أن is governed by تأمرك and the second is coordinated with ما in ما يعبد.
[TAB-FULL:v12p546#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض القراء | reports | Some readers are reported to read ما تشاء, making the second أن clause coordinate directly with the first.
[TAB-FULL:v12p546#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari says the hostile people used الحليم الرشيد sarcastically to mock, belittle, and portray Shuaib as foolish.
[TAB-FULL:v12p546#2/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj says their description of Shuaib as forbearing and rightly guided was mockery.
[TAB-FULL:v12p546#2/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd likewise says they mocked him by calling him forbearing and rightly guided.
[TAB-FULL:v12p546/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · زيد بن أسلم | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam reports that clipping dirhams was among the things Shuaib forbade.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p72/r10] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · التفسير | reports | A reported explanation says Shuʿayb forbade them to clip or break coins.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p72/r11] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قيل | reports | One explanation is that they used praise ironically to mean that he was foolish and ignorant.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p72/r12] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قيل | reports | Another view is that they said it mockingly.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p72/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | A variant reading is aṣalawātuka, with a long ā in ṣalawāt.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p72/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Their response shows that they worshipped gods other than God.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p72/r9] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Their complaint means that they had agreed among themselves to shortchange in their business dealings.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2072#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الأعمش | reports | Al-A'mash glosses your prayers as your recitation.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2072#2/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says Shuayb's prayers really did command his people to abandon what their forefathers worshiped.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2072#2/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · زيد بن أسلم | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam says they were forbidden to shave small amounts off coins, which he calls corruption in the land.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2072#2/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatada glosses the phrase as doing whatever they desire.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2072#2/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سفيان الثوري | reports | Sufyan al-Thawri says the phrase refers to zakat.

[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2072#2/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ميمون بن مهران | reports | Maymun ibn Mihran says the phrase was spoken in mockery.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2072#2/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says the people were mocking the Prophet.
[NAHHAS:v2p298/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisa'i parses the first أن as genitive after an understood باء.

[THALABI:v5p186/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · القاضي | reports | The judge explains that Arabs sometimes call something by its opposite as a favorable omen or euphemism, as when they call a bitten person safe or a mouse a place of escape.
[THALABI:v5p186/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Another view takes the phrase as mockery, like ironic names or the firekeepers' address to Abu Jahl; the author cites the latter's scriptural wording. | mentions 44:49

[THALABI:v5p186/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن كيسان | reports | Ibn Kaysan takes the description literally: Shuayb is forbearing and rightly guided, so it ill suits him to break his people's unity or oppose their religion. | mentions 11:62
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الأعمش | reports | Al-Aʿmash glosses ṣalāt as recitation.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words as a denial: they mean Shuʿayb is neither forbearing nor rightly guided.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن بحر | reports | Ibn Baḥr says they sincerely concede Shuʿayb’s wisdom, then ask why he forbids them their desired conduct with their property.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | It may mean Shuʿayb’s devotional prayer to God.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | It may mean his religion, which he was ordered to follow; ṣalāt’s root sense is following, as in the horse-racing term al-muṣallī.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The question can mean that Shuʿayb’s prayer calls him to their way.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Alternatively, the question asks whether his prayer commands them to abandon the idols and images their ancestors worshipped.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One explanation is that their desired conduct was cheating in weights and measures.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · زيد بن أسلم وسفيان الثوري | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam and Sufyān al-Thawrī say Shuʿayb commanded them to pay zakat, which they refused.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · زيد بن أسلم | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam says Shuʿayb also forbade them from clipping coins.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v2p496/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says they called him wise and rightly guided sarcastically.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p54/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | People who fail to understand treat their acts as small, but the gravity of an act comes from opposing the Almighty, not from its size; a little lawful provision is better than much that ends in ruin. | mentions 24:15
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p523/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The word is also read in the singular; the discussion of both readings was given under 9:103. | mentions 9:103
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p523/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عطاء عن ابن عباس | reports | They mean: does your religion command you? Prayer stands for religion because they saw it as a religious practice.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p523/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan gives the same interpretation: they ask whether his religion commands him.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p523/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Another report from Ibn Abbas says Shuayb prayed often, which is why they spoke of his prayer.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p523/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | reports | Their statement shows they worshiped gods other than God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p523/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | Prayer does not literally command; it causes the action associated with it, as in 29:45, because prayer is part of faith and faith restrains wrongdoing. | mentions 29:45

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p525/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The ancestors are dead, but their past worship is expressed in the present tense and means what they used to worship, as in 2:102. | mentions 2:102

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p526/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو بكر | holds | Abu Bakr says the ironic interpretation fits Arabic usage: calling someone sensible can mean he is a fool or ignorant.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p526/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الشاعر | reports | An anonymous poet's ironic address يا حليم is clarified by the line's ending, which shows the addressee was being called ignorant.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p526/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل بن سليمان | reports | Muqatil explains the ironic words as foolish and astray.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p416/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The Companions witnessed revelation and knew its interpretation as native speakers of Arabic.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p416/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The Successors and early pious authorities did not contrive their collections or strain to chase remote hidden meanings.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p416/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Scholars of meanings focused on grammatical parsing and explaining modes of discourse; later writers differ in rank and purpose, and few closely align wording with exegesis in a consistent, fluent way.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p416/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Although earlier scholars left little unexplored, later authors can gather scattered pearls with subtle skill, arranging them attractively and earning praise and reward.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p416/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Wāḥidī says he worked to establish the discipline's foundations and learned language from Aḥmad b. Muḥammad al-ʿArūḍī, a veteran lexicographer who studied and transmitted from major language authorities including al-Azharī.

[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p83/r5] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · أبو حفص الشطرنجي | reports | Abū Ḥafṣ al-Shatranjī wrote the poem in the voice of ʿUlayya, Hārūn al-Rashīd’s sister, after al-Rashīd reproached her.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p83/r6] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The position of قد كنت أحسب in Abū Ḥafṣ’s poem is an example of the placement of a resumption.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p83/r7] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | In Abū Duwād’s horse poem, the author points to the indefinite رماحا as a meaningful choice of wording.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p83/r8] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Ibn al-Bawwāb’s four lines are added as another poetic specimen in this discussion of arrangement; this excerpt does not single out a particular feature in them.
[JISHUMI:v5p3551/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · حمزة، والكسائي، وحفص عن عاصم | reports | Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from Asim read the singular صلاة without waw, while the others read the plural صلوات.
[JISHUMI:v5p3551/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · بعضهم | reports | The common reading has the speakers say we do what we wish; some read both verbs with ta, meaning Shu'ayb commands what they do with their wealth, a construction the author says is more apt but not to be read in both forms.
[JISHUMI:v5p3551/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The phrase is not coordinated with the first أن; it coordinates with ما, yielding the sense of leaving them free to act in their wealth as they wish.
[JISHUMI:v5p3551/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | An alternative parse treats the command as a prohibition: the people ask whether prayer commands one thing and forbids another, returning the coordination to the first أن.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The worship practiced by their ancestors refers to idols.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says Shuʿayb prayed often, prompting their remark about his prayer.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الأعمش | reports | Al-Aʿmash interprets the word as your recitation.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Their claim about doing as they wished with their wealth includes increasing and decreasing it.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · قيل | reports | Another report says Shuʿayb forbade clipping dinars and dirhams, calling it unlawful, and they objected that they could do as they wished with their money.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says they meant the opposites, foolish and misguided; Arabs may name something by its opposite, as in calling a bitten person sound or a desert a salvation.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · قيل | reports | Another view takes their words as mockery.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · قيل | reports | Another explanation is that they called him forbearing and right-guided according to his own claim.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p195#2/r9] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · قيل | reports | A literal reading has them call Shuʿayb forbearing and right-guided among his people and argue he should not divide them by opposing their religion; they use the same reproach made to Ṣāliḥ in 11:62. | mentions 11:62
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Shuʿayb prayed often; when his people saw him praying, they exchanged glances and laughed, so their question mocks his worship.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Prayer can metaphorically command or forbid good, as in 29:45, but the people deliberately cast it as a ridiculous command to ridicule Shuʿayb's prayer. | mentions 29:45
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | They imply that abandoning idols has no rational basis and must come from delirium or satanic obsession, which they associate with his constant prayers.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The construction means your prayer commands us with the charge to abandon ancestral worship; التكليف is elided because one person is not commanded to perform another's act.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | A variant reads the word in the singular, أصلاتك.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads both verbs with direct address: أو أن تفعل في أموالنا ما تشاء, referring to Shuʿayb's prohibition of fraud and counsel to accept lawful earnings.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Shuʿayb urged them to stop shortchanging and accept a small lawful gain rather than a large forbidden one; another report says he forbade clipping coins.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r8] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | They ironically call Shuʿayb supremely foolish and astray, reversing praise as one might sarcastically call a miser Hatim.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p395#2/r9] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قيل | reports | Alternatively, they say he is reputed among his people for patience and right guidance, implying his commands contradict that reputation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الناس | reports | The majority read both verbs with first-person plural nūn. Al-Dahhak reads both with second-person tāʾ; Abu Abd al-Rahman reports nūn then tāʾ, as does Ibn Abbas.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | Another view has them mean that Shuayb is forbearing and rightly guided only in his own estimation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | A further view takes the praise literally as their belief, then makes it a rebuke: a truly wise man should not issue such commands.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report says that when the Prophet addressed Banu Qurayza as ‘brothers of apes,’ they replied, ‘Muhammad, we never knew you to be ignorant.’ Ibn Atiyya compares the gentleness of Shuayb’s speech with Muhammad’s address.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | With nūn in both verbs, the second ‘an’ coordinates with ‘what,’ not the first ‘an’; otherwise the sense becomes ‘Does your prayer command us to do whatever we wish with our property?’
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · بعض النحويين | reports | Some grammarians allow the second ‘an’ in the tāʾ reading to coordinate with ‘what’; they also allow coordination to the first ‘an’.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | rejects | Ibn Atiyya objects that ‘leave’ means ‘abandon’ in the first clause but ‘allow’ in the second, so the parsing requires semantic variation or an omitted noun; nūn-then-tāʾ cannot coordinate the second ‘an’ with ‘what’ without reversing the sense.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The apparent reference to what they do with their property is the short measure and weight already mentioned.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · محمد بن كعب وغيره | reports | Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and others say the phrase alludes to clipping dirhams and dinars and fraudulently passing them alongside genuine coins.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab calls clipping coins corruption in the land; this is interpreted as the fraud described or changing coinage to consume people’s wealth.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | One interpretation is that they actually called Shuayb ignorant and foolish, while God veiled their insult with the opposite wording.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن جريج وابن زيد | reports | Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd say these were their exact words, spoken sarcastically.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور الناس | reports | The majority read ‘your prayers’ in the plural, while Ibn Waththab reads it in the singular; he likewise uses the singular in the cited verses. | mentions 9:9, 23:9
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · فرقة | reports | One group understands Shuayb’s prayer as the familiar prescribed prayers; a report says he was the most prayerful of the prophets.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الحسن | reports | Hasan says God imposed prayer and almsgiving on every prophet.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قيل | reports | Other interpretations take ‘your prayers’ to mean Shuayb’s recitation, his mosques, or his supplications.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | Ibn Atiyya finds the prescribed prayers a

nd supplications likeliest: their rank in prayer is represented as urging Shuayb to denounce their religion and customs, as prayer restrains indecency. | mentions 29:45
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p200/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Their complaint explicitly shows that their ancestors worshipped gods other than God.
[TABRISI:11:84-95/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | Alternatively they meant the praise sincerely: as a patient leader among his people, he should not oppose them.
[TABRISI:11:84-95/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Ḥalīm is one who does not hasten to punish someone who deserves it; rashīd is one who guides.
[TABRISI:11:84-95/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | The people mocked Shuʿayb's appeal because he prayed often and taught that prayer restrains evil and forbids indecency and wrongdoing.
[TABRISI:11:84-95/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن وعطاء وأبو مسلم | reports | They meant ‘does your religion command you’; prayer stands for religion because it is among its most important practices.
[TABRISI:11:84-95/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | They spoke about Shuʿayb's prayer in mockery.
[TABRISI:11:84-95/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | They ask whether his prayer commands them to leave their fathers' worship or to stop doing what they wish with their wealth, including cheating and short measure.
[TABRISI:11:84-95/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | On one view the praise is sarcastic and means the opposite: foolish and astray.
[TABRISI:11:87/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · أهل الكوفة غير أبي بكر | reports | The Kufans except Abū Bakr read the word in the singular, without wāw.
[TABRISI:11:87/r17] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | An-nasb in أو أن نفعل means ‘or [does it command] that we do’; it coordinates with ما يعبد آباؤنا, not أن نترك, which would make the sense defective.
[TABRISI:11:87/r18] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Here أو has the alternative force of ‘sit with al-Ḥasan or Ibn Sīrīn’ and the cited statement that God is nearer to either rich or poor. | mentions 4:135
[TABRISI:11:87/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · الباقون | reports | The remaining readers use the plural form with wāw.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p346/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Sayyid originally means one elevated by leadership and rank.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p346/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | The second sense is a forbearing or gentle master; the source groups with it the phrase about John in 3:39. | mentions 3:39
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p351/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Sulūk originally means entering, and it is extended metaphorically where context indicates another sense.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p393/r12] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | reports | Shuʿayb’s people use ṣalāt to mean his religion.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p3/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The Qur'an honors the community, guides people by God's enabling, reforms them through promise and warning, and is protected from ignorant alteration and hostile distortion.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p3/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The Qur'an's challenge to all humans and jinn to produce its like is cited at 17:88. | mentions 17:88
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p3/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Muhammad was sent to people near and far as bearer of good tidings and warning, a shining lamp, and recipient of abundant favor; he has no equal among his kind.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p3/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The Qur'an is the noblest field of knowledge, so understanding its meanings is the highest form of understanding; the worth of knowledge follows the worth of its subject.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p3/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Ibn al-Jawzī found large tafsirs inaccessible, short ones incomplete, and medium works disorganized and often inattentive to difficult passages.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p3/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | He wrote this concise tafsir to contain substantial knowledge, compressed its wording, and urges the reader to memorize it, seeking God's help.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p3/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿūd says the Companions learned ten verses from the Messenger at a time and did not move on until they understood their knowledge and practice.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p3/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan, transmitted by Qatāda, said he wanted to know the occasion and intended meaning of every verse God revealed.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · حمزة والكسائي وخلف وحفص | reports | Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf, and Ḥafṣ read ṣalātuka in the singular.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · سفيان الثوري | reports | Sufyān al-Thawrī says this reading means Shuʿayb ordered them to give zakāt and they refused.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي والضحاك وابن أبي عبلة | reports | Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read both verbs in the second person, with the same meaning as al-Fihrī's reading.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو صالح عن ابن عباس وقتادة والفراء | reports | Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and al-Farrāʾ say the people spoke sarcastically.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says they used the phrase ironically to call Shuʿayb foolish and ignorant.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو الحسن المصيصي | reports | Abū al-Ḥasan al-Muṣīṣī says they insulted Shuʿayb as neither forbearing nor rightly guided, while God affirms that he truly is both.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r15] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الماوردي وابن كيسان | reports | Al-Māwardī and Ibn Kaysān say they sincerely acknowledged Shuʿayb's forbearance and sound guidance, then challenged his authority over their property.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عطاء | reports | ʿAṭāʾ interprets Shuʿayb's ṣalāt as his religion.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الأعمش | reports | Al-Aʿmash interprets it as Shuʿayb's recitation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | A third view takes it as the familiar ritual prayers, noting that Shuʿayb prayed often.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ construes the question as asking whether Shuʿayb's prayers command them to abandon ancestral worship or to abandon doing as they wish with their wealth.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says their conduct with their wealth was fraud and short measure, which they regarded as mutually agreed.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says they cut dirhams and dinars.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · القرظي | reports | Al-Quraẓī reports that they were punished for clipping dirhams.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p149/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الضحاك بن قيس الفهري | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays al-Fihrī reads the verb in the second person, mā tashāʾ, and coordinates it with an tatruka without ellipsis.
[RAZI-FULL:v16p142/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الباقون | reports | The remaining readers use the plural in the parallel Hūd phrase as well. | mentions 11:87
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One interpretation is sarcastic inversion: they call Shuʿayb foolish and ignorant while using the opposite words.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second reading is that he was considered forbearing and right-guided in his own eyes or by his people.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Razi prefers that they acknowledge Shuʿayb was renowned for sound judgment, then mockingly ask how such a man can forbid their ancestral religion.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم | reports | Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, and Hafs from Asim read the word in the singular without wāw; the remaining readers read it plural with wāw.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Shuʿayb had called them to monotheism and to abandon fraud; their reference to leaving their fathers’ worship answers the first demand, while their question about their money answers the second.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Their appeal to their ancestors is adherence to inherited custom by sheer imitation.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One interpretation takes prayer as religion and faith, since it is religion’s most visible emblem; alternatively, its root evokes following, as the racehorse المصلي follows the leader, so the phrase means ‘your religion commands you.’
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, they mean the formal prayers: Shuʿayb prayed often, and his people sarcastically mocked him when they saw him praying, as one might mock someone who attributes foolish speech to his reading.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | To explain the syntax, one may supply ‘that we leave doing what we wish,’ coordinating the phrase with what their fathers worshipped.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, prayer both commands them to abandon idols and forbids them from doing whatever they wish with their money.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p36/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads both verbs in the second person, ‘or that you do with our wealth what you wish’; this refers to Shuʿayb’s demand to stop short measure and fraud and accept little lawful gain over abundant unlawful gain.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-95/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Mālik says they broke dinars and dirhams; earlier exegetes including Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and Zayd ibn Aslam say the same, and breaking them is a grave sin.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:84-95/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-ʿArabī distinguishes clipping, which reduces coin value and secretly takes property
